list.listitem: Children should routinely be vaccinated against measles with two doses of MMR: first dose between 12 and 15 months and the second dose at 4 to 6 years or at least 28 days following the first dose. A
Adolescents and adults who have not had measles and have not been vaccinated should receive at least one dose of MMR and preferably a second dose of MMR given at least 28 days later. A
Suspect measles in all persons who are not known to be immune to measles who present with fever, generalized rash, and cough. C

In patients with suspected measles, submit acute and convalescent serum for antimeasles IgG and IgM and submit urine and throat or nasal swab for viral isolation. Measles RNA can also be detected by real-time polymerase chain reaction (PCR) from a nasopharyngeal swab and used for confirming measles infection. C
Treat infected patients with supportive care and symptom management. C

background.definition: Measles (rubeola) is a highly infectious exanthematous respiratory disease characterized by fever, cough, malaise, and a pathognomonic exanthem on the buccal mucosa. It is caused by the measles virus, a single-stranded, RNA virus with one serotype. Humans are the only natural host.

list.listitem: Worldwide, there are an estimated 20 million cases of measles each year. The global death rate from measles has decreased from 0.63 million in 1990 to 0.13 million in 2010.
Before the introduction of vaccination in 1963, approximately 3 to 4 million persons had measles annually in the United States.

In 2000, the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) declared that measles had been eliminated from the United States. Since then there have been sporadic confirmed cases of imported measles and measles largely in patients who were unvaccinated or had unknown or undocumented vaccination status.

Among US residents, 1789 measles cases were reported from 2001 to 2015 for an annual incidence ranging between 0.08 (95% CI, 0.05-0.12) and 2.06 (95% CI, 1.91-2.22) per million population compared with a worldwide incidence of 40/million population. Most (73.4%) cases were acquired in the US and occurred in those who were unvaccinated (69.5%).

In 2019, there was a large increase in measles cases with 1,282 individual cases confirmed in 31 states by the CDC. This was the highest incidence since 2010; in 2014, 667 cases of measles were reported.

In the 2019 outbreak, 89% of cases were unvaccinated or had unknown vaccination status. Median age of cases was 6 years, 13% were infants and 29% were adults age 18 years or older. Ten percent were hospitalized, 60 cases (5%) had pneumonia and one person had encephalitis; no patients died.

Between March 24, 2014 and July 23, 2014, 383 outbreak-related cases of measles were reported in nine counties in Ohio, primarily among Amish individuals. The median age of case patients was 15 years (range, <1-53); most (89%) were unvaccinated. The outbreak originated from two unvaccinated Amish men who had returned to the United States from the Philippines.

In the measles outbreak in Minnesota in 2011, there were 21 confirmed cases with a median age of 12 months (range, 4 months to 51 years); over half (67%) were hospitalized. The first patient recognized was a child without a travel history and the index case was a 30-month-old US-born child infected while visiting Kenya. Over 3000 individuals were exposed. Sixteen case-patients were unvaccinated despite 9 of the 16 being age-eligible.

In large measles outbreaks in Lyon, France, in 2010 and 2011, 407 cases were diagnosed. The most common age groups were children <1 year of age (32%) followed by individuals between 17 and 29 years old (31%). Seventy two (18%) had complications.

In a large outbreak in 2011 in Quebec, Canada, there were 21 measles importations and 725 cases, with 1 importation resulting in sustained transmission and 678 cases. The highest incidence was in adolescents 12 to 17 years old (75.6 per 100,000) of whom many did not receive two-dose MMR. Two-dose recipients had milder illness and a significantly lower hospitalization risk than those unvaccinated or who were single-dose recipients.

An economic analyses of the 2009 US birth cohort showed that routine childhood immunization prevents about 20 million cases of disease and 42,000 early deaths, with a net savings of $13.5 billion in direct costs and $68.8 billion in total societal costs.

Authors of a systematic review and meta-analysis designed to estimate the rate of measles susceptibility among healthcare workers in Italy found an overall prevalence of susceptibility of 11.5% (95% CI, 8.1-15.4) and susceptibility by direct evaluation of blood specimens of 9.1% (95% CI, 6.2-12.5).
Caused by the measles virus which is a member of the genus Morbillivirus and of the family Paramyxoviridae.
The virus is transmitted via airborne droplets or direct contact with respiratory secretions from an infected individual.
Measles virus RNA has also been identified in air and surface specimens in the hospital room of a patient admitted with measles. It is not clear if virus can be transmitted by fomites.
The virus invades cells of the respiratory mucosa and is then spreads to the reticuloendothelial system via the bloodstream where it proceeds to infect white blood cells, particularly monocytes.
The disease can be transmitted from 4 days prior to the onset of rash to 4 days after the rash appears. The infectivity of the virus peaks during the prodromal phase of the illness.
Genetic sequencing (hemagglutinin and matrix genes) can be performed to determine links between outbreaks.
Children should routinely be vaccinated against measles with two doses of MMR: first dose between 12 and 15 months of age and the second dose at 4 to 6 years of age. A

In a review of 18 published measles studies describing 1416 measles cases, of the 970 measles cases with detailed vaccination data, 574 cases (59.2%) were unvaccinated despite being vaccine eligible and 405 (70.6%) of these had nonmedical exemptions.

For children traveling internationally from the US, the CDC recommends administering one dose of MMR vaccine to infants aged 6 through 11 months before departure from the United States for international travel. For children aged 12 months and older, two doses should be provided prior to departure—the first administered on or after age 12 months and the second dose at least 4 weeks later. Additional instruction can be found on the CDC immunization webpage. C

Adverse effects include febrile seizures within 2 weeks and thrombocytopenic purpura within 6 weeks. Exposure to the MMR vaccine is unlikely to be associated with other diseases including autism, type 1 diabetes, Crohn's disease, and demyelinating diseases. Receiving a primary DTP after measles vaccine is associated with increased mortality for female, but not for male children. Overall, serious vaccine-associated side effects are extremely rare.
Serologic screening for measles does not need to be done before vaccinating and is not necessary or cost-effective for persons who have already been vaccinated. C

The CDC states that acceptable presumptive evidence of immunity against measles includes at least one of the following: written documentation of adequate vaccination, laboratory evidence of immunity, laboratory confirmation of measles, or birth before 1957.

Unvaccinated adolescents and adults born after 1957 should receive at least one dose of MMR. A second dose should be given at least 28 days later. Persons born before 1957 can be assumed to be immune to measles. A
Quarantining close contacts of cases can reduce transmission. A

Single-dose vaccination: Authors of a Cochrane review found one MMR vaccine dose was 95% effective in preventing clinical measles, 81% effective in preventing secondary cases among household contacts, and 74% effective (at least one dose) in preventing measles after exposure (post-exposure prophylaxis). Clinical effectiveness after two doses of MMR was 96%.
Two-dose vaccination: The CDC estimates a 97% effectiveness for the two-dose MMR vaccine.

In a Danish population-based cohort study of 495,987 children, receipt of the MMR on schedule after the third dose of DTaP-IPV-Hib, vs. DTaP-IPV-Hib as the most recent vaccine, was associated with a lower rate of hospital admissions for any infection (4.6% vs. 5.1%; adjusted incidence rate ratio 0.86 [95% CI, 0.84-0.88]).

Authors of a meta-analysis of 62 studies found a seroconversion rate to the measles vaccine of 96.0% (95% CI, 94.5-97.4) and overall annual waning rates of 0.009 (95% CI, 0.005-0.016). There was high study heterogeneity however.

Early vaccination: An early 2-dose measles vaccination schedule (first dose at 4.5-9 months) was found to be associated with protective measles virus antibody levels at 24 months of age in nearly all children in one study.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 56 studies found a seroconversion rate of 50% (95% CI, 29-71) for infants vaccinated with the first measles-containing vaccine (MCV1) at 4 months of age increasing to 85% (69-97) for those were vaccinated at 8 months. Authors of a second meta-analysis also found older age at MCV1, from 6 to ≥15 months, improved antibody response and measles protection among one-dose recipients. In this study, serological studies reported high seropositivity regardless of age at administration of MCV1 while epidemiological data suggested lower protection with earlier age at MCV1, based on a few studies.

In a population cohort in the Netherlands who were offered early vaccination between 6 and 14 months during a measles outbreak, vaccinated infants had a lower risk of confirmed measles than unvaccinated infants (3 vs. 10 cases). Unadjusted vaccine efficacy was 94%, but efficacy adjusted for religion and sibling's vaccination status decreased to 71% indicating that part of the effect was caused by herd immunity.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 13 studies found that overall administering MCV1 to infants younger than 9 months followed by additional MCV doses resulted in high seropositivity, vaccine effectiveness, and T-cell responses. One study however, found lower antibody titers after one or two subsequent doses of MCV when measles vaccination is started at less than 9 months of age.

Co-vaccination with Haemophilus influenzae and varicella vaccines does not negatively affect immunologic response or appear to increase adverse effects to MMR. Similarly, co-vaccination of tetravalent MMR/varicella (MMRV) vaccine with hepatitis A vaccine and 7-valent pneumococcal conjugate vaccine appears safe and effective, although seroresponse rates were not fully demonstrated for varicella-zoster virus. Co-vaccination using MMRV with MenACWY-CRM did not affect the immune response to either vaccine.
Using the MMR-varicella (MMRV) vaccine instead of the MMR and separate varicella vaccine, one additional child will experience a febrile seizure for every 2300 children vaccinated.

Delayed vaccination: In a cohort of 323, 247 US children from the Vaccine Safety Datalink, delaying the first MMR vaccine past 15 months of age results in a higher risk of seizures (incident rate ratio 2.65 [95% CI, 1.99-3.55] with vaccination at 12-15 months and 6.53 [95% CI, 3.15-13.53] with vaccination at 16-23 months).

Special populations: Measles vaccines appear safe and effective in HIV-infected children; in one meta-analysis, 59% of HIV-infected children (95% CI, 46%-71%) were seropositive after receiving standard-titer measles vaccine at 6, 9, or 12 months. No serious adverse events were reported in over half the studies.

Authors of an updated meta-analysis found 4 of 12 studies demonstrating statistically significant reductions in seropositivity among HIV-infected children compared with HIV-uninfected children within 4 months of vaccination, with forest plots in 2 studies showing decreasing immunity over time.

Measles seroprevalence among HIV-infected adolescents and adults, however, is high (median, 92%; 27 studies) with no significant difference compared to HIV-uninfected participants making additional doses of measles vaccine likely unnecessary.

Among children with juvenile idiopathic arthritis who had undergone primary immunization, MMR booster vaccination (vs. no booster) was immunogenic and did not worsen disease activity. Biologic treatments were discontinued at 5 times their half-lives prior to vaccination.
Increasing vaccination uptake: Encouraging parents to vaccinate their child by emphasizing direct benefits to the child rather than societal benefits may increase vaccine uptake.
Pretravel consultations are a potential opportunity to provide vaccination against measles.

Cochrane authors concluded that use of patient reminder and recall systems in primary care settings appear effective for improving receipt of immunizations (risk ratio 1.28; 95% CI, 1.23-1.35). These include postcards, text messages, or autodialer based on high-certainty evidence, and telephone calls and letters to patients based on moderate-certainty evidence.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 9 papers found technological (e.g., visually-enhanced education materials, social marketing strategies), mass marketing or campaigning (e.g., storytelling), and direct communication approaches matched to perceived barriers to be helpful for increasing vaccine uptake.
Suspect measles in all persons who are not known to be immune to measles who present with fever, generalized rash, and cough. C
In patients with suspected measles, submit acute and convalescent serum for antimeasles IgG and IgM. C
Submit urine and throat or nasal swab for viral isolation. C

Differential.Differential_Features: Children <3 years old, 2-3 mm macules start on trunk, spare face
Rash tends to clear from affected areas as it migrates, may be pruritic
Blanchable erythema on cheeks, perioral pallor, then diffuse rash on trunk
Occurs in previously vaccinated persons, rash begins on extremities, spreads to trunk

list.listitem: summarizes the constellation of symptoms and physical findings associated with different phases of acute measles infection.

A pathognomonic exanthem, Koplik's spots, occurs during the prodrome, and is characterized by 1- to 3-mm grayish elevated spots with an erythematous base on buccal mucosa. In one case series of all suspected measles cases reported to the North-West London Health Protection Unit over a 6-month period, the PV+ of clinical suspicion of measles was 50%; using the presence of Koplik’s spots improved the PV+ to 80% (OR of measles in the presence of Koplik’s spots was 7.2 [95% CI, 2.1-24.9]).

During the exanthem phase, a morbilliform rash begins on the face and spreads centrifugally to the neck, trunk, and extremities. It rarely involves the palms and soles. The rash will become brownish and begin to fade.
Neutropenia and lymphopenia are common laboratory findings. Leukocytosis may indicate a bacterial superinfection.

Antimeasles serum IgM is recommended by the World Health Organization as the standard test to confirm suspected measles. It is detectable 3 days after appearance of rash. False positives may be caused by human parvovirus B19 IgM.

The CDC also notes that measles RNA detected by real-time PCR in a respiratory specimen (nasopharyngeal swab) is a common method for confirming measles infection. Molecular analysis can also be conducted to determine the genotype of the measles virus which is used to map transmission pathways of measles viruses.
Antimeasles IgG peaks 14 days after the rash appears.

In countries with a low prevalence of measles, both acute and convalescent sera should be tested for antimeasles IgM and IgG to decrease false positive results. A fourfold increase in antimeasles antibody titer is indicative of infection.
Atypical measles characterized by extremely high measles antibody titer by day 10 of illness.
A urine specimen and throat or nasal swab should also be submitted for viral isolation as soon as possible after the rash appears.
Suspect measles in unvaccinated persons who present with a prodrome characterized by fever and general malaise followed by cough, coryza, and conjunctivitis followed by the characteristic exanthem.
summarizes phases of infection and associated symptoms and signs.

Atypical measles may occur in individuals who were vaccinated with a formalin-inactivated measles vaccine in the US between 1963 and 1967 and are subsequently exposed to measles. Characterized by peripheral rash which spreads centrally.
The CDC recommends confirming suspected cases of measles with serological testing.

The CDC also recommends post-exposure prophylaxis with MMR vaccine, if administered within 72 hours of initial measles exposure, or immunoglobulin (IG), if administered within six days of exposure, to individuals exposed to measles who cannot readily show that they have evidence of immunity; this may provide some protection or modify the clinical course of disease.
Supportive care and treatment of symptoms with adequate hydration and acetaminophen. C
Vitamin A may be beneficial in some severe cases of measles. B
All suspected cases of measles should be reported to the state department of health. C
Isolate patients for 4 days after they develop the measles rash. C
Follow airborne precautions in hospital. C
Treatment is generally supportive and symptom-based. Patients should maintain adequate hydration. Acetaminophen may be used for fever or other discomfort.

Authors of a Cochrane review of seven trials with 1263 children comparing antibiotics with placebo or no treatment to prevent complications of measles found a significant difference in the development of pneumonia (removing one older trial; OR 0.26; 95% CI, 0.12-0.60; NNT 18 to prevent one episode), purulent otitis media (OR 0.34; 95% CI, 0.16-0.73), and tonsillitis (OR 0.08; 95% CI, 0.01-0.72). No major adverse events were reported. Data are limited, however, and it is not possible to recommend the type of antibiotic (options include penicillin or co-trimoxazole), duration, or the day of initiation.

Two doses of vitamin A given on consecutive days reduce mortality risk, especially in children younger than 2 years, patients with known vitamin A deficiency, or those who are severely malnourished. One only needs to treat between 7 and 60 children with vitamin A to prevent one death from measles.

Single doses should be given on each of 2 consecutive days to children with severe cases of measles: 50,000 IU vitamin A for children 1 to 5 months old, 100,000 IU for children 6 to 12 months old, 200,000 IU for children 12 months and older.

Although vitamin A deficiency predisposes to more severe keratitis, corneal scarring, and blindness from measles, it is not known whether supplementing with vitamin A will prevent blindness in children with measles.

In one small RCT of 100 persons with measles, treatment with ribavirin (a nucleoside inhibitor) vs. supportive care only significantly reduced duration and severity of fever and constitutional symptoms (e.g., anorexia, malaise, conjunctivitis, cough, rash), complication rate, and duration of hospital stay.
No randomized trials of Chinese medicinal herbs for treating measles exist.
All suspected cases of measles should be reported to the state health department.
Severe cases of measles or those with complications may need to be hospitalized. About 1 in 5 unvaccinated people with measles requires hospitalization (CDC).
The most common complications of measles are otitis media, (about 1 in 10 children) and diarrhea (less than 1 in 10 children) according to the CDC.

More severe complications include secondary bacterial or viral pneumonia, tracheobronchitis,postinfectious encephalomyelitis, and subacute sclerosing panencephalitis (SSPE); 1/1000 measles cases develop acute encephalitis and 7 to 11 out of every 100,000 are estimated to be at risk for SSPE.
Bacterial pneumonia and otitis media: usually are due to superinfection and should be treated with appropriate antibiotics.
Postinfectious encephalomyelitis: autoimmune response in the recovery phase that causes demyelination, presents with fever, headache, neck stiffness, seizures, and altered mental status.

SSPE: slowly progressive, eventually fatal disease that develops 7 to 10 years after measles infection, results in degeneration of the central nervous system. While care is generally supportive, a neurologist should be consulted.
Measles/mumps-attributed pancreatitis has been reported and occurred in 3.8% of viral-attributed pancreatitis cases in one systematic review.
summarizes the natural course of measles infection; clinical improvement typically occurs 3 to 4 days after rash appears, although cough may persist for up to 2 weeks. C
Disease is generally self-limiting, although approximately 20% of cases may be complicated by pneumonia, otitis media, or subacute sclerosing panencephalitis. B

Measles is fatal in 1 to 2 per 1000 patients, generally from respiratory and neurologic complications. B Authors of a systematic review and modeling analysis reported a mean case-fatality ratio of 2.2% (95% CI, 0.7-4.5) for 1990-2015. Case fatality ratios were lower in community-based vs. hospital-based settings (1.5% vs. 2.9%).

Although measles vaccine is contraindicated during pregnancy, there were 131 reports of MMR vaccine administration to pregnant women in the 2003 to 2013 Vaccine Adverse Event Reporting System; no adverse effects were reported. Data on safety of MMR in pregnancy are lacking.

Measles is rare in pregnancy but can cause miscarriage, stillbirth, preterm birth and low birth weight. In the 2011 measles outbreak in France noted above, 11 pregnant women were hospitalized with measles infection. The most severe maternal complication was pneumonia, which occurred in 4 women; all women delivered healthy newborns. Post-exposure prophylaxis was initiated for three newborns whose mothers acquired measles in the immediate postpartum period. None of these newborns subsequently acquired measles, despite breastfeeding.

Authors of a meta-analysis of 29 papers from 1941 to 2012 with 420 cases of measles in pregnant women reported 8 deaths (4.3%) with the most frequent complication being pneumonia (75/420, 17.9%). Fifty-five births of 410 cases (13.4%) with available data were preterm.

Breastfeeding provides some protection against measles. In a British cohort study, breastfeeding for >3 months vs. never breast fed was negatively associated with a diagnosis of clinical measles infection after adjustment for crowding, social class, measles vaccination, parity and sex with an OR of 0.69 (95% CI, 0.60-0.81).

In the general population of mostly vaccinated women, the estimated duration of protection by maternal antibodies among infants is 3.3 months for measles, 2.7 months for mumps, 3.9 months for rubella, and 3.4 months for varicella.

In a study in the Netherlands, early vaccination offered during an outbreak to children 6 to 14 months was well tolerated with the lowest reporting of systemic adverse effects among infants aged 6-8 months (32% vs. 45% and 43% for older infants).
